genres.working_definition: Dub is the Jamaican reggae-derived studio practice and genre built by stripping and recomposing an existing riddim: vocals and instruments are removed, fragmented, or dropped in and out while bass, drums, spatial echo, reverb, filtering, and the mixing desk itself become compositional elements. This dossier follows that lineage from 1970s Jamaica through UK and international soundsystem continuities.
explicit_exclusions: Exclude a generic Dub Mix or Dub Version suffix when the underlying rhythm, scene, and production remain part of another genre.
Exclude vocal-led roots Reggae recordings whose song performance remains primary rather than being deconstructed at the mixing desk.
Exclude Dub Techno when a steady techno pulse, looped chord stabs, and club-tempo structure dominate the reggae riddim.
Exclude Dubstep and Future Garage when half-time 140-derived bass-music rhythm and drop structure dominate.
Do not split Dub Reggae or Reggae Dub into separate targets; both are compatibility aliases for this canonical genre.

genres.working_definition: Electro is the machine-funk and electro-funk lineage formed in the early 1980s where hip-hop and funk practice met synthesizers, sequencers, vocoders, and especially syncopated TR-808 rhythm programming. The dossier follows that lineage through Detroit and European revivals while preserving its broken-beat, robotic center.
explicit_exclusions: Exclude Electro House and later festival EDM uses of the shortened word electro.
Exclude Synth-pop, EBM, and Electroclash when song form, industrial body rhythm, or rock-pop presentation dominates the machine-funk lineage.
Exclude Detroit Techno when a straight four-to-the-floor pulse and techno scene identity dominate.
Do not use electro as a generic synonym for electronic music.

research_caveats: Electro has repeatedly been diluted into a generic electronic prefix; candidate selection follows the broken-beat electro-funk lineage rather than current marketing shorthand.
Detroit electro and Detroit techno overlap historically and institutionally; four-to-the-floor Model 500 material is retained only as explicit boundary review.
The 1990s European revival overlaps Electroclash, Synth-pop, EBM, and Italo Disco, so song form and scene history must be considered alongside drum programming.

genres.working_definition: A broad UK Garage reference set centered on the early four-to-the-floor and vocal sound that developed from pitched-up US garage house in mid-1990s Britain, then fed the wider late-1990s and early-2000s UKG continuum. Because the catalog separately names 2-Step Garage and Speed Garage, tracks whose defining identity is one of those styles are boundaries rather than central Garage anchors.
explicit_exclusions: Exclude the US Garage House and Paradise Garage sense of the word when it is not part of the UK lineage.
Exclude garage rock and other non-electronic uses of Garage.
Treat clearly dominant 2-Step Garage and Speed Garage records as boundaries because both are separate catalog genres.
Exclude Bassline, Future Garage, UK Funky, Grime, and Dubstep when their later scene identity dominates the audio.

genres.working_definition: Hardcore is the high-speed electronic rave lineage that emerged around 1990 from tougher techno, acid, industrial, new beat, and related club strains, with distorted or otherwise forceful kick drums as a persistent center. This operational dossier follows the live taxonomy's broad Hardcore target through early, mainstream, millennium, industrial, terror, and uptempo continuities while keeping neighboring canonical genres separate.
explicit_exclusions: Exclude hardcore punk, metal, and other guitar-led uses of hardcore.
Exclude UK breakbeat hardcore when its chopped-break and soundsystem lineage is better represented by Jungle or Happy Hardcore.
Keep Gabber as the separate early Rotterdam and Dutch scene-specific target already present in the taxonomy.
Keep Happy Hardcore, Hardstyle, Hard Trance, Hard Techno, and Jungle as separate canonical targets rather than absorbing them into this umbrella.
Do not classify a track as Hardcore merely because it is hard or fast.

genres.working_definition: Tech House is a historically shifting house-tempo club lineage first incubated in early-1990s London as a DJ practice joining the swing, funk, and low end of house with techno's tougher, stripped, or Detroit-derived texture. It became a production category by the late 1990s, absorbed West Coast tribal, minimal, and electro-house traits in the 2000s, and expanded into a polished big-room and festival category in the 2010s. Across eras, the classifier target retains a four-on-the-floor house pulse, low-end groove, stripped or repetitive arrangement, and techno-leaning drums or textures; evidence must be evaluated in its historical context.
explicit_exclusions: Exclude generic House or Deep House whose harmony, vocals, and soulful song structure dominate without the stripped, tougher, techno-derived rhythmic character.
Exclude Techno when a straighter machine pulse, harder attack, and reduced house swing or funk dominate the recording.
Exclude Minimal or Minimal Techno when sparse repetition is the only evidence; Tech House also requires house-tempo groove and the relevant scene or release context.
Exclude Progressive House when long-form melodic development and sweeping harmonic builds dominate over compact, groove-led repetition.
Do not use the current Beatport chart identity to rewrite the genre's broader 1990s DJ-led lineage.
